title: Hakeem Jeffries overwhelmingly wins House speaker nomination despite threats from ultra-progressives | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Hakeem Jeffries is now all but certain to lead the House next January, a role that will make him the first Black speaker in US history as he oversees Democrats’ largest majority in years.

Roughly two weeks after their midterms romp, House Democrats voted to back Jeffries for the top job in the new Congress, despite some on the far-left clamoring for new leadership.

A small bloc of newly elected Democratic socialists had refused to publicly commit to Jeffries ahead of the leadership election, demanding concessions like votes for Medicare for All or a ban on arms sales to Israel.

But in the end, just 11 Democrats voted against him in the secret ballot vote, according to a source familiar with the vote, all but ensuring he will win the gavel in the new Congress.

“People of this country are demanding big, dramatic and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable. And we’re committed to delivering in a meaningful way the type of change that the American people deserve,” Jeffries told reporters after clinching the nomination.

A group of seven ultra-progressive new members declared in a statement that they voted “no” because they are still seeking commitment from Jeffries on key priorities, including votes on Medicare for All and ending “the genocide in Gaza,” they said. Signed onto the statement were Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.

Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard told CNN that he also voted against nominating Jeffries for speaker, emphasizing that he wants commitments that Jeffries will prioritize key issues like money in politics and blocking US aid to Israel.

“We’re looking for a strong commitment to end the Citizens United this Congress through a 28th Amendment, and we’re looking to call a vote on US aid to Israel,” said Leonard. “Until I get confirmation on those votes he does not have my support. We’ve got until the first week of January, I’m still holding out hope.”

Valdez later told CNN that she needed to “stand up” for the voters who elected her earlier this month: “I think there’s a lot that’s still on the table right now, and I’m really eager to continue conversations and fighting for everything we can at this moment.”

Asked about the defectors, Jeffries would say only: “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other.”

But other Democrats were more blunt about their frustrations. Rep. Hillary Scholten, a centrist from Michigan, complained that “infighting over leadership positions” would not help deliver on their campaign promises.

“There’s even still a few that you know didn’t want to own up to how they voted,” she said, calling out “a lot of disorganization in that segment of the caucus right now.”

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who faced her own defectors during her leadership runs, downplayed the impact of those 11 Democratic “no” votes.

“I’m glad he took the vote so people could see how small the opposition was to him,” she said.“Don’t make a big deal. Each one of them is important. As 11, not so important compared to 250 some votes that he received,” she said.

Moments before he formally clinched the nomination, Jeffries received a powerful endorsement inside the room from Rep. Jim Clyburn, a longtime ally and one of the most senior members of the Congressional Black Caucus.

“Hakeem is interested in headways and not headlines,” Clyburn declared in his signature baritone voice, according to two people in the room, delivering a speech that one described as “powerful” as the caucus formally nominated the nation’s first Black speaker.

Now, all that stands between Jeffries and the gavel is a formal vote by the full chamber on the floor on January 3 — the first act of the new Congress — which his allies, and even his detractors, expect he will easily survive.

His leadership team will include Rep. Katherine Clark, who is set to become House majority leader – the first woman to hold that job – and Rep. Pete Aguilar, who will be the first Latino in history to hold the House’s No. 3 job of whip.

Democrats’ only competitive leadership election of the day – the vice chair position – also yielded a historic result. Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois will become the highest-ranking Black woman in Congress.

Inside the room, Underwood – who’s earned respect in the party for her heads-down approach to legislating – made a remark that was viewed by some fellow Democrats as a criticism of her competitor for the slot, Rep. Sara Jacobs.

“Being wealthy is not the primary or important qualification for leadership,” Underwood said in a speech just ahead of the vote, according to two people in the room.

Jeffries had always been expected to coast through the party vote on Wednesday, because the Democrats’ majority next year is simply too large for any small bloc of lawmakers to hold sway. But people close to the New York Democrat insist that he took nothing for granted.

Ahead of the election, he lined up face-to-face conversations with any incoming Democrats who had refused to commit — nearly all aligned with the Democratic Socialists for America. He sat down with the biggest factions of his caucus, including the centrists, New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dog Caucus, as well as the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

Jeffries and his team have kept their private discussions closely guarded. But Democrats have noted some subtle shifts in Jeffries’ public remarks, including a significant shift on one of the left’s biggest policy demands: Medicare for All.

Jeffries announcedon Fridaythat he backs major tenets of a universal healthcare system, specifically, lowering the eligibility age for Medicare, creating a new program that guarantees universal coverage for kids and adding hearing, dental and vision coverage to the program.

It’s a major nod to progressive priorities, mirroring Sen. Bernie Sanders’ approach to a phase-in for Medicare for All system. (Centrist Democrats, meanwhile, have pushed for a Medicare-like public option.)

This story has been updated with additional developments.

CNN’s Manu Raju and Annie Grayer contributed to this report.

CNN’s Manu Raju and Annie Grayer contributed to this report.
